scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that self-interest drives much behaviour while arguing genuine selflessness exists; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: People often argue that even kindness is secretly selfish at its root.
One claim holds that no act is done purely for others, on the reason that all actions are ultimately based on self-interest.
I agree that self-interest drives much of what we do, but I disagree that no act is ever truly selfless.
First, there is real truth in the reason that self-interest shapes many of our actions.
Even generous acts often bring us rewards, such as praise, gratitude, or a good feeling.
For example, a person may give to charity partly to feel proud or to look good to others.
This shows that hidden self-interest can lie behind acts that seem purely kind.
Much of human behaviour really is driven by the wish for benefit or comfort.
We naturally tend to protect ourselves and to seek our own advantage.
To this extent, the reason behind the claim has genuine force.
Second, however, some acts truly are done purely for the benefit of others.
People sometimes sacrifice greatly for strangers with no possible reward to themselves.
Consider a person who dies trying to save a drowning stranger she will never meet again.
Such sacrifice cannot be explained away as mere hidden self-interest.
To call every kind act selfish stretches the idea of self-interest until it means nothing.
Quiet, anonymous giving, expecting no thanks, also shows that real selflessness exists.
Genuine concern for others, then, is a real part of human nature.
In conclusion, self-interest does drive a great deal of what we do.
But some acts are genuinely selfless, done purely for the good of others.
Human nature includes both deep self-interest and a real capacity for selfless care.
